entry: Navigable sea route in southern Chile separating mainland [[South America]] from the [[Tierra del Fuego]] archipelago. The strait is an important natural passage between the Atlantic and Pacific oceans, about 570 km (350 mi) long and 2 km (1.2 mi) wide at its narrowest point. Indigenous peoples, including the Kawésqar, Tehuelche, Selkʼnam and Yaghan, have lived around it for at least 13,000 years. The expedition of Portuguese navigator [[Ferdinand Magellan]] brought the first Europeans to the area in 1520. Magellan named it Estrecho de Todos los Santos ("Strait of All Saints"), but King Charles V of Spain, who had sponsored the voyage, renamed it for him. Narrows and unpredictable winds make navigation difficult, and maritime piloting is compulsory. It is more sheltered than the [[Drake Passage]] around [[Cape Horn]], which is beset by gales and icebergs. Before the construction of the [[Panama Canal]], it was one of the few sea routes between the two oceans.

Narrow waterway between the [[Malay Peninsula]] and the Indonesian island of [[Sumatra]]. It is about 900 km (560 mi) long and 65 to 250 km (40 to 155 mi) wide, connecting the Andaman Sea of the [[Indian Ocean]] with the South China Sea. Over 94,000 vessels passed through it in 2008, making it the busiest strait in the world, and it carries approximately 25% of the world's traded goods, including oil. As of 2024, over 35% of seaborne oil and 20% of gas flows pass through it. Heavy traffic makes [[Piracy|piracy]] and smuggling a concern. In the 7th century the maritime empire of [[Srivijaya]], based in Palembang, gained effective control of the strait and dominated the region for about 700 years. Later powers included the [[Malacca Sultanate]], the Johor Sultanate, the British Straits Settlements and the city-state of [[Singapore]].

Clade of mostly single-celled [[Eukaryote|eukaryotes]], also called heterokonts, distinguished by stiff tripartite external hairs. In most species the hairs are attached to [[Flagellum|flagella]], and they have been lost in some groups, such as most [[Diatom|diatoms]]. Stramenopiles are one of three major clades in the SAR supergroup, alongside Alveolata and [[Rhizaria]]. The group includes algal protists, heterotrophic flagellates and [[Oomycete|oomycetes]], and some large seaweeds, such as the [[Brown algae|brown algae]]. The name was introduced by D. J. Patterson in 1989 to define a group overlapping the ambiguous heterokonts, and it was formalized in 2005.

headword: Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde
sort_key: strange case of dr jekyll and mr hyde
entry: Gothic horror novella by [[Robert Louis Stevenson]], published in 1886. London [[Lawyer|lawyer]] Gabriel John Utterson investigates strange occurrences involving his friend Dr Henry Jekyll and the murderous Edward Hyde. Considered a defining work of Gothic literature, it explores [[Good and evil|good and evil]] within a single personality. Stevenson later wrote that a dream gave him its central idea, a voluntary change becoming involuntary. Within six months of publication it sold over 40,000 copies. The phrase "Jekyll and Hyde" denotes someone outwardly good but sometimes shockingly evil.

American television series created by the Duffer Brothers for [[Netflix]] (2016–2025). Set in the 1980s in the town of Hawkins, [[Indiana]], it follows residents after a psychokinetic girl named Eleven inadvertently creates a wormhole to the Upside Down, an alternate dimension. Blending horror, science fiction and coming-of-age drama, it draws on 1980s pop culture and on the work of [[Steven Spielberg]], [[John Carpenter]] and [[Stephen King]]. Reviewers praised its characterization, atmosphere and homage to 1980s cinema. It drew record viewership for Netflix and spawned a stage play, *The First Shadow* (2023), books, comics and a [[Dungeons & Dragons]] role-playing starter set.

City (pop., 2023: 294,229), prefecture of the Bas-Rhin department and largest city in the Grand Est region of northeastern France. It lies in the historic region of [[Alsace]] and is the official seat of the [[European Parliament]]. The [[Council of Europe]], which includes the European Court of Human Rights, is also based there. Together with [[Geneva]] and [[New York City]], it is one of the few cities that are not national capitals but host international organizations of the first order. Its historic Grande Île was designated a [[World Heritage Site]] by [[UNESCO]] in 1988, and the newer Neustadt was added in 2017. Violently disputed throughout its history, it has long been a cultural bridge between France and Germany, and its port is the second largest on the [[Rhine]], after Duisburg.

[[Board game|Strategy board game]] for two players, played on a 10×10 board. Each player commands an [[Army|army]] of 40 pieces marked with Napoleonic insignia, and wins by capturing the opponent's [[Flag|flag]] or by capturing all movable enemy pieces. The game is a slightly modified copy of the early 20th-century French game *L'Attaque* ("The Attack"). The name was first registered in 1942 in the [[Netherlands]], and the game has been produced in Europe since [[World War II]] and in the [[United States]] since 1961.

Branch of [[Geology|geology]] concerned with rock layers (strata) and their stratification, used mainly for sedimentary and layered volcanic rocks. It has three subfields: lithostratigraphy, based on physical rock type; biostratigraphy, based on fossil content; and chronostratigraphy, based on age. Its theoretical basis was set by Nicholas Steno in 1669, with the law of superposition, which holds that in an undeformed sequence the oldest strata lie at the base. William Smith applied it on a large scale in the 1790s, using fossil markers to correlate strata and producing the first geological map of England. Biostratigraphy was one of the first powerful lines of evidence for [[Evolution|biological evolution]], and the [[Geologic time scale]] was developed from it in the 19th century before radiometric dating gave it an absolute framework.

Second-lowest layer of Earth's atmosphere, above the troposphere and below the mesosphere. Temperature rises with altitude because the [[Ozone|ozone]] layer absorbs the Sun's [[Ultraviolet|ultraviolet]] radiation, unlike the troposphere below. Its lower edge is as high as 20 km (66,000 ft) near the [[Equator]] and about 7 km (23,000 ft) at the poles. Temperatures range from an average of −51 °C near the tropopause to −15 °C near the mesosphere. Winds can reach about 60 m/s (220 km/h) in the Southern [[Polar vortex|polar vortex]], far stronger than in the troposphere.

Steep, conical volcano built of alternating layers of hardened [[Lava|lava]] and tephra, also called a composite volcano. Unlike [[Shield volcano|shield volcanoes]], they have steep profiles and summit craters, and their viscous lava cools before spreading far. More than 700 have erupted lava during the [[Holocene]] epoch, and they are typically found at subduction zones, such as the [[Andes]]. [[Krakatoa]] in Indonesia erupted in 1883, claiming 36,000 lives; [[Mount Vesuvius]] in Italy erupted in AD 79, killing an estimated 2,000 people. [[Mount St. Helens]] (1980) in Washington state and [[Mount Pinatubo]] (1991) in the Philippines also erupted catastrophically, with fewer deaths.

Edible fruit of the garden strawberry, a widely grown [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrid]] plant in the [[Rosaceae|rose family]]. Botanically it is an aggregate accessory fruit rather than a [[Berry (botany)|berry]], and its apparent seeds are achenes. The garden strawberry was first bred in Brittany, France, in the 1750s from the North American Virginia strawberry and the Chilean strawberry, which had reached Europe in 1714. In 1766 Antoine Nicolas Duchesne showed, in the gardens of the [[Palace of Versailles]], that it was a hybrid. Strawberries appear in literature from Roman times, when [[Virgil]] wrote of a snake hidden beneath one. They also appear in paintings, such as [[Hieronymus Bosch]]'s *The Garden of Earthly Delights*. World production exceeded ten million tons in 2024, led by China with 38% of the total.

Method of delivering [[Multimedia|multimedia]] through a network for playback in real time or near real time. Data arrive as a stream of packets from a server to a client, rather than as a complete file that must be downloaded first. Online streaming was popularized by RealNetworks and [[Microsoft]] in the 1990s and has become the most popular way to consume music and video worldwide. Numerous subscription services have competed since the 2010s, including [[Netflix]]. Live streaming delivers content in real time during production, much as a television broadcast does.

Fighting video game by Capcom, released for arcades in 1991 as the second *Street Fighter* installment. Designed by Yoshiki Okamoto and Akira Yasuda, it added special-command moves, a combo system and a six-button layout. It is widely cited as the most influential fighting game, popularizing the genre in the 1990s. Its two-player mode inspired tournaments culminating in the Evolution Championship Series. The [[Super Nintendo Entertainment System]] port sold more than 6.3 million cartridges, Capcom's best-selling single game for 20 years. Its major successor was *Street Fighter III*, released in 1997.

Branch of engineering mechanics that calculates [[Stress (mechanics)|stresses]] and strains in structural members such as beams, columns and shafts. It predicts how structures respond to loads and fail, using material properties such as yield strength, ultimate strength, [[Young's modulus]] and Poisson's ratio, along with member geometry. Transverse loads bend a member, while axial loads stretch or shorten it. Strength is a material's ability to withstand an applied load without failure or plastic [[Deformation (engineering)|deformation]]. Yield stress marks the point beyond which deformation is not fully reversed, and ultimate strength is the maximum stress reached. The field began with one- and two-dimensional members and was later generalized to three dimensions; Stephen Timoshenko was an important founding pioneer.

Suborder of [[Primate|primates]] comprising the [[Lemur|lemurs]] of Madagascar, the [[Galago|galagos]] and pottos of Africa, and the lorises of India and Southeast Asia. Strepsirrhines have a moist rhinarium, large olfactory lobes and a vomeronasal organ that detects [[Pheromone|pheromones]]. Unlike haplorhine primates, they produce their own [[Vitamin C|vitamin C]]. Lemuriforms have a toothcomb used for grooming, and most living lemuriforms are nocturnal. Extinct adapiform relatives thrived in Europe, North America and Asia during the [[Eocene]]. Lemurs reached Madagascar from Africa between 47 and 54 million years ago, and lorises split from African galagos around 40 million years ago. Many living strepsirrhines are endangered by habitat destruction, hunting for bushmeat and the exotic pet trade.

Organism's response to a stressor, such as an environmental condition or change in life circumstances. In humans and most mammals, the autonomic [[Nervous system|nervous system]] and the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis are the two main systems that respond. The sympathetic system can trigger fight-or-flight, and the HPA axis regulates [[Cortisol]], which influences metabolic, psychological and immune functions. Chronic stress is a common risk factor for mental illness and for [[Disease|disease]], including coronary heart disease. Some people remain healthy despite chronic stress; vulnerability depends on genetic and psychological factors and on the age at which stress occurs. Acute severe stress can cause derealization, depersonalization and [[Anxiety|anxiety]].

Physical quantity in [[Continuum mechanics|continuum mechanics]] describing the internal forces within a material, expressed as force per unit area. It is measured in [[Pascal (unit)|pascals]] (newtons per square meter). A stretched elastic band is under tensile stress, and a crumpled sponge under compressive stress. Stress expresses the forces that neighboring particles exert on each other, while strain measures relative deformation. Stress beyond a material's strength limits causes permanent deformation, fracture or changes in its crystal structure. Built-in stress, as in prestressed concrete and tempered glass, can exist without external forces. The scientific understanding of stress became possible only in the 17th and 18th centuries, with the work of [[Galileo Galilei]] and [[René Descartes]].

Class of [[Musical instrument|musical instruments]] that produce sound from vibrating strings, also called chordophones. Bowed instruments such as the [[Violin]] form the core of the [[Orchestra]], while the [[Harp]] and [[Guitar]] are played mainly by plucking. Curt Sachs reduced chordophones to four basic kinds: zithers, lutes, [[Lyre|lyres]] and harps. Most have a hollow body that projects the sound, although an electric guitar may have a solid body and rely on an amplifier. Some of the earliest known string instruments, harps and lyres from [[Mesopotamia]], date to the third millennium BCE, and the violin family has been central to symphony orchestras since the Baroque era.

Theoretical framework in [[Physics|physics]] that replaces point-like [[Elementary particle|particles]] with one-dimensional vibrating strings. Different vibrational states of a string correspond to different particles, one of which is the [[Graviton]], which carries gravity; the theory is therefore a theory of [[Quantum gravity]]. It has contributed to the study of [[Black hole|black holes]] and early-universe cosmology, and it is a candidate for a [[Theory of everything|theory of everything]]. The theory was first studied in the late 1960s as a theory of the strong nuclear force before its promise for gravity emerged. Five consistent superstring theories were linked in the mid-1990s as limiting cases of a single eleven-dimensional theory, [[M-theory]]. Some in the field criticize the theory because the full version lacks a satisfactory definition in all circumstances and describes an enormous landscape of possible universes.

American politician and [[United States Senate|United States senator]] from [[South Carolina]], serving 1954–2003. An avid segregationist, he ran as the States' Rights Democratic ("Dixiecrat") presidential candidate in 1948, finishing third with 2.4% of the popular vote. In 1957 he completed the longest single-person Senate filibuster, 24 hours and 18 minutes, against the Civil Rights Act of 1957. He opposed the Civil Rights Act of 1964, switched to the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]] and endorsed [[Barry Goldwater]]. As a Republican he served three times as president pro tempore. He retired in 2003 as the only member of Congress to reach age 100 while in office.

Chemical element with symbol Sr and atomic number 38, an [[Alkaline earth metal|alkaline earth metal]]. Strontium resembles [[Calcium|calcium]] and [[Barium|barium]] in its properties and is highly reactive, forming a dark oxide layer in air. It occurs mainly in the [[Mineral|minerals]] celestine and strontianite, the latter named for Strontian, Scotland, where it was found in 1790. [[Humphry Davy]] first isolated the metal in 1808 by [[Electrolysis|electrolysis]]. In the 19th century it was mostly used to refine sugar from [[Sugar beet|sugar beets]]. At its peak, as much as 75% of U.S. strontium consumption went into television tube faceplate glass. Natural strontium is stable, but the radioactive isotope strontium-90 is one of the most dangerous components of nuclear fallout, because the body absorbs it like calcium.

Highly toxic, bitter, crystalline [[Alkaloid|alkaloid]] used as a [[Pesticide|pesticide]], particularly against small vertebrates. It is extracted from the seeds of the *Strychnos nux-vomica* tree. Poisoning causes muscular convulsions and death by [[Asphyxia|asphyxia]]. Once given in small doses as a heart and bowel [[Stimulant|stimulant]] and performance enhancer, it is no longer used medicinally. Its use as a [[Rodent|rodent]] poison is restricted or banned in many regions because of risks to non-target wildlife. Its complex molecular structure has made it a demanding synthetic target, and [[Robert Burns Woodward]] was an early chemist to target its synthesis.

Person enrolled in a [[School|school]] or other educational institution, or one who takes a special interest in a subject. In the [[United Kingdom]] and most Commonwealth countries, a student attends secondary school or higher, while those in primary school are pupils. Systems vary by country. [[Nigeria]] uses a 6-3-3-4 system of six years of primary school, three of junior secondary, three of senior secondary and usually four of university. Primary education is compulsory for six years in [[Singapore]], and for children aged six to ten in [[Bangladesh]]. In [[Cambodia]], a [[Bachelor's degree|bachelor's degree]] normally takes four years.

Symmetric, bell-shaped [[Probability distribution|probability distribution]] that generalizes the [[Normal distribution|normal distribution]]. Its tails are heavier, controlled by ν, the number of degrees of freedom; at ν = 1 it becomes the Cauchy distribution, and as ν grows it approaches the normal distribution. The name "Student" was a pseudonym of William Sealy Gosset, who worked at the Guinness brewery in [[Dublin]]. It underlies the [[Student's t-test|t-test]] and [[Confidence interval|confidence intervals]] for means, and it appears in [[Regression analysis|linear regression]].

Statistical test of whether the difference between two groups is significant. A test is a Student's t-test when its test statistic follows a [[Student's t-distribution|t-distribution]] under the null hypothesis, which holds under certain conditions when a scaling term such as the [[Standard deviation|standard deviation]] is estimated from data rather than known. Its most common use is to test whether two population means differ. The one-sample version compares a sample mean with a hypothesized value, with n − 1 degrees of freedom. For large datasets it gives results very similar to a Z-test. The test was introduced in 1908 by William Sealy Gosset, who published under the pseudonym "Student" in the journal *Biometrika* while working at the Guinness brewery in [[Dublin]], Ireland. [[Ronald Fisher]]'s work made it widely known.
